messages.ds: No relabeling or retraining needed. We add the synonym list, re-index the retriever and re-run the evaluation set, which is about 1–2 days. It should reduce retrieval misses on Arabic/English package names and help accuracy, but I have no measured gain. AI Engineer components do not need to change.
messages.engineer: No code change is needed on the engine side. The synonym list is applied in the knowledge base and retriever, and the answer, guardrail, handover and channel components keep their interfaces. We would only run a short regression check of the price check and Arabic answers, about 0.25–0.5 days. Handover (median 22 s) and the refund and billing-dispute rules are not affected.
messages.domain: No domain document needs to change, so 0 days for Domain. The change breaks no rule (no refund promises, billing disputes still go to a human). I'd review the synonym list to check each Arabic name maps to the correct official package. This is a review only, and the list should follow the weekly catalogue refresh.

cases.alternative: Bot acknowledges the double-charge complaint without promising anything and hands over to a human agent within the 30 s limit; the agent decides on the refund

messages.engineer: The bot can't offer a refund for double charges. That breaks "never promise refunds" and "billing disputes always go to a human agent". The safer option is for the bot to acknowledge the double charge and hand over to an agent straight away, which is about 1 day of engine work. The 2–4 day estimate for the original change is my own, not based on a past change.
messages.domain: The bot offering a refund breaks two rules: "never promise refunds" (r-refund) and "billing disputes always go to a human agent" (r-dispute). A double-charge complaint is a billing dispute. Don't ship it. The bot should acknowledge the complaint politely and hand over to a human agent, who decides on any refund. No domain document needs to change, and our review takes 0 days.

messages.ds: Only the retriever changes on the DS side. No relabeling or retraining is needed, but we must re-run the full evaluation before release, which takes about 1.5–2 days. Accuracy is the top priority and has only 1.2 points of headroom (91.2% against the 90% target). Keyword matching probably helps with Arabic/English package names, and we have no data showing that vector-only search holds accuracy, so I can't promise the metric stays above target.
messages.engineer: The engine interfaces don't change, so we only need to re-test the answer guardrails (price check, sensitive-topic and billing-dispute detection), handover and channel latency. That is about 1–2 days. The main risk is accuracy: it is 91.2% against a 90% target, and vector-only search may miss exact plan names and prices. The Data Scientist should show offline accuracy results before this ships, and no recorded rule is broken.
messages.domain: No domain document, guideline or annotation has to change, so the domain effort is 0 days. I only need to review the result. The rules on billing disputes going to a human (r-dispute) and never promising refunds (r-refund) are not changed by this. Accuracy is the top priority, and I have no evidence on whether vector-only retrieval is as good at exact terms like package names and prices. The Data Scientist should check it on the existing test questions before release, and the reason for the change was not given.

messages.engineer: The model swap mainly changes the Answer + guardrails engine (about 2 days). We must re-test first-token p95 (limit 2 s, now 1.4 s) on the app and WhatsApp, and re-check that the handover (median 22 s, limit 30 s) still triggers. The AI team must confirm the new model keeps the billing-dispute handover and never-promise-refunds behaviour. No reason was given and I have no record of a past model swap, so this range is an estimate.
messages.domain: No domain document or guideline has to change for a model swap, so the domain effort is 0 days, and a review alone doesn't count. The new model must still never promise refunds (r-refund) and must still hand over every billing dispute (r-dispute). Please re-run those refund and dispute test cases before go-live. No reason for the change was given.

cases.alternative: Post-processing rule: helmet counts only if its box overlaps the top part of a head box (no relabeling or retraining; untested, effort is my estimate; needs validation on the 400-image eval set)

messages.ds: This needs a new annotation guide version, relabeling of existing images, retraining YOLOv8n and re-checking the 400-image evaluation set, about 4-6 DS days. The change respects r-worn and keeps the model on YOLOv8n, so CPU latency should not change. I have no data on how it moves recall or false alerts, and no past relabel to anchor the estimate. A cheaper untested option is a post-processing rule: a helmet counts only if its box overlaps the top of a head box, with no retraining.
messages.engineer: A new class for carried helmets means the compliance logic must treat it as a violation, and the app's reason text must add a "helmet carried, not worn" message. This is 3-4 days for Engineering, including re-testing on all camera feeds. It doesn't break any rule: it supports r-worn, and YOLOv8n stays CPU-safe. It depends on the Data Scientist's retrained model v3 arriving with the final class name.
messages.domain: The helmet rule itself stays the same, because a carried helmet is already a violation. I would only add a note to the rule text that the new "carried helmet" class counts as a violation, which is 0.5–1 day. Compliance logic must alert on that class. If it is treated as compliant or ignored, r-worn breaks and violation recall drops. No reason was given for the change, so please confirm the goal. The retrain effort and the 3-week pilot date are for the Data and AI teams and the Lead to check.

cases.alternative: Keep YOLOv8n v3 (head recall 96% already meets the ≥95% target) and improve it with hard-negative data or threshold tuning, checked on the 400-image eval set

messages.ds: YOLOv8s needs retraining and re-evaluation on the 400-image set (about 2–3 DS days). It breaks the engine contract that edge boxes are CPU-only and models larger than YOLOv8n miss latency. We already tested it in Exp 4: mAP50 rose from 0.89 to 0.91, but it was 2.3x slower, so we parked it. Keep YOLOv8n v3, which already has 96% head recall.
messages.engineer: YOLOv8s breaks the engine contract (e-cpu): the CPU-only edge boxes can't meet latency for all 40 cameras with any model larger than YOLOv8n, which puts the 60 s alert limit and the 3-week pilot (p-pilot) at risk. The output format and class names don't change, so the compliance logic and app need only re-testing, about 1–3 days. That is only if the hardware question is settled first, and I have no evidence that new hardware is available. I'd keep YOLOv8n and improve accuracy by fine-tuning it or tuning its thresholds.
messages.domain: No domain document (annotation guide, rules) has to change, so my effort is 0 days, only a review. But the Engine contract (e-cpu) says models larger than YOLOv8n miss the latency limit on CPU-only edge boxes, so YOLOv8s puts the 60 s alert and the pilot promise at risk. No reason was given for the upgrade. The "worn on head" rule (r-worn) is about labels and logic, and a bigger model won't fix it.

cases.alternative: Tune the confidence threshold on labelled site footage to meet both recall ≥95% and <10 false alerts/camera/day. Route borderline detections to a low-priority review list instead of instant alerts.

messages.engineer: The change touches the compliance logic (new low-confidence branch) and the safety app (alert and reason text), about 2-3 days. Alerting on every low-confidence head detection will probably push false alerts above ~10 per camera per day (r-fatigue), and I have no data to size it. Safer option: set a tuned confidence threshold on pilot data and show low-confidence cases as a separate "needs review" alert type.
messages.domain: No domain document needs to change (0 days, review only). Alerting on every low-confidence head detection will probably push false alerts above the agreed ~10 per camera per day (r-fatigue). That risks officers ignoring alerts, which hurts safety and the recall goal. Safer option: tune the confidence threshold on site data to keep recall at 95% or higher. Send borderline detections to a non-alerting review list, not to the alert feed.

cases.alternative: Run the untested post-processing rule (a helmet counts only if its box overlaps the top of the head box). It needs no retraining, but it addresses false alerts and the 'worn' rule, not small-head recall.

messages.ds: DS needs to label the 1,000 crops, retrain YOLOv8n and re-run the evaluation, which is about 3.5–5.5 days. The model stays YOLOv8n, so CPU latency is not affected, and the AI Engineer needs no code change unless the new model changes the thresholds. I can't claim a recall gain yet, because no past test supports one. Recall and false alerts must be re-measured on the 400-image site evaluation set, and the crops must stay out of that set.
messages.engineer: No code change is needed on the engine side if the retrained model stays YOLOv8n with the same classes and output format. We would re-run the compliance logic and app alerts on the new model's output, mainly to check small far-away boxes, which is about 0.5–1.5 days. If the model's classes change or tiling is added at inference time, the latency (60 s) and CPU-only limits need to be re-checked.
messages.domain: No domain document has to change, so the effort is 0 days. I only need a short review. The new crops should be labelled under Annotation guide v1 and the "helmet counts only when worn on the head" rule (r-worn). Far-away heads help violation recall, which is the top priority. Data Scientist should check the false-alert rate (under ~10 per camera per day) on the evaluation set, because small crops can add false positives.

cases.alternative: Keep hard safety rules on top of the LLM classifier (design A, current design); tune the LLM only for routine and mixed messages

messages.ds: Removing the hard safety rules breaks the head nurse's "always emergency" list and the under-2 nurse rule, and it gives up the 100% emergency recall we measured with the rules in place. With only about 120 emergency examples, the LLM alone can't be shown to be safe. We would have to retrain and re-evaluate, and we recommend keeping the rules as a safety layer on top of the LLM.
messages.engineer: Removing the hard safety rules breaks the head nurse's always-emergency list (r-emergency) and the child-under-2 nurse callback (r-child). Nothing would be left to stop an LLM miss from reaching the booking tool or skipping the nurse alert. We would have to rework the booking guard, the nurse-alert trigger and the WhatsApp reply path, about 2-4 days, and 100% emergency recall could no longer be guaranteed. Keep the rules on top of the LLM (design A) instead.
messages.domain: Blocked on safety: removing the hard rules lets the LLM alone decide which symptoms are emergencies. That breaks the head nurse's approved always-emergency list (r-emergency) and the under-2 nurse rule (r-child), and risks missed emergencies or appointments offered to emergency patients. No domain documents need to change (0 days). Keep the rule-based checks on top of the classifier. The LLM can still judge urgency for everything the rules don't cover.

messages.ds: This breaks the head nurse's rule r-child: any child under 2 must get a nurse callback within 1 hour, and the agent can't change that clinical rule alone. Agent A keeps routing under-2 cases to a nurse. If nurse workload is the concern, raise it with the head nurse. I'm not estimating effort for this change because it shouldn't be built as proposed.
messages.engineer: This breaks the head nurse's rule r-child (any child under 2 gets a nurse callback within 1 hour) and the project constraint that any child under 2 goes to a nurse. Engineering should not build it. If the aim is lower nurse workload, change the nurse-callback handling and keep nurse routing for under-2s, but that needs the head nurse's agreement first.
messages.domain: This breaks the head nurse's rule r-child: any child under 2 must get a nurse callback within 1 hour, so it can't go to a same-day appointment instead. No domain document changes, so the effort is 0 days. To cut nurse workload, keep the nurse route and look at faster triage tools for the nurse. Any change to the under-2 rule needs the head nurse's agreement first.

cases.alternative: Keep instant alerts for emergencies and child-under-2 cases; only group or digest lower-priority notifications, subject to head nurse approval

messages.engineer: Batching nurse alerts every 15 minutes breaks the engine contract that every nurse alert arrives within 30 seconds, and it would delay emergency and child-under-2 alerts by up to 15 minutes. Rework is about 2–3 days (alert sender, plus WhatsApp channel flow and tests), and no reason for the change was given. Safer option: keep emergency and child-under-2 alerts instant, and batch only low-urgency notifications if alert noise is the concern.
messages.domain: No domain documents need to change (review only, 0 days), but I block this. A 15-minute batch could delay emergency nurse alerts (chest pain, stroke signs, seizure) by up to 15 minutes. That breaks the 30-second nurse-alert requirement and the always-emergency rule r-emergency, which says to alert a nurse. Keep emergency and under-2 alerts immediate, and batch only lower-urgency items if the aim is to reduce noise. The head nurse would need to agree to that.
